prompt: `var monday` holds a `StudySession` whose `course` is declared with `let`. What does `monday.course = "Kotlin"` do?
hint: The instance is a `var`; the property is not.

choices.text: Changes the course, as `monday` is a `var`
choices.why: A `let` property is fixed at initialisation whatever holds the instance.

choices.text: It is refused at compile time
choices.why: Right: `cannot assign to property: 'course' is a 'let' constant`.

choices.text: Compiles, and crashes when the line runs
choices.why: It never runs.

choices.text: Creates a new session with the new course and keeps the old one
choices.why: Assignment does not create instances.

prompt: `struct StudySession { let course: String; var minutes: Int; var done = false }`. Which call compiles?
hint: A default value makes its argument optional.

choices.text: `StudySession(minutes: 45, course: "Swift")`
choices.why: The memberwise arguments come in declaration order.

choices.text: `StudySession(course: "Swift")`
choices.why: `minutes` has no default, so it is required.

choices.text: `StudySession(course: "Swift", minutes: 45)`
choices.why: Right: `done` may be left out and takes `false`.

choices.text: `StudySession("Swift", 45)`
choices.why: The memberwise initialiser has labels.

prompt: Which of these can a `let` stored property of a struct be given a value by? Choose all that apply.
hint: Once, when the instance is made.

choices.text: A default value in its declaration
choices.why: Yes, and then it gets no initialiser argument.

choices.text: A line in an `init`
choices.why: Yes: the initialiser is where a constant is not yet fixed.

choices.text: A `mutating` method
choices.why: No: after initialisation a `let` property never changes.

choices.text: A `didSet` observer
choices.why: No: observers are for `var` properties.

prompt: `Week(sessions: [45, 30])` with `goal = 300` and `remaining` computed as `max(goal - total, 0)`. After `week.sessions.append(60)`, what is `week.remaining`?
hint: The total is recomputed on each read.

prompt: `var hours: Double { get { Double(minutes) / 60 } set { minutes = Int(newValue * 60) } }`. After `session.hours = 1.25`, where is the 1.25 kept?

choices.text: In `hours`, beside `minutes`
choices.why: `hours` has no storage at all.

choices.text: Nowhere: `minutes` holds 75, and `hours` computes 1.25 again on each read
choices.why: Right: the setter translated the value into the stored property.

choices.text: In `newValue`, until the next assignment
choices.why: `newValue` exists only while the setter runs.

choices.text: Nowhere: computed properties cannot be assigned
choices.why: This one has a `set`, so it can.

prompt: A teammate stores `total` as a `var` and updates it in every method that adds a session. What failure does a computed `total` rule out?

choices.text: Reading `total` too often
choices.why: A computed property is read as often as you like.

choices.text: An overflow when the total passes `Int.max`
choices.why: Both versions add the same numbers.

choices.text: A total that disagrees with the sessions
choices.why: Right: one forgotten update is enough, and a computed property has nothing to forget.

choices.text: A struct that cannot be compared with `==`
choices.why: Stored or computed, `Equatable` works the same.

prompt: `var minutes: Int { didSet { … } }`. Does the observer run when `StudySession(minutes: 45)` is created?
hint: What did `Observers.swift` print when the session was made?

choices.text: Yes, with `oldValue` 0
choices.why: There is no old value during initialisation, and nothing printed.

choices.text: Yes, but only `willSet`
choices.why: Neither observer ran.

choices.text: No
choices.why: Right: observers run on assignments to an instance that already exists.

choices.text: Only when the struct is held in a `var`
choices.why: `session` was a `var`, and still nothing printed at creation.

prompt: With `didSet { if minutes > 600 { minutes = 600 } }`, what does `minutes` hold after `session.minutes = 900`?
Inside `didSet`, the value the property held before the assignment is called `___`.
A `lazy var summary` prints "building the summary" when its value is built. The program reads `summary` twice. How many times is that line printed?

choices.text: Twice, once per read
choices.why: That is a computed property; a lazy one stores what it built.

choices.text: Once, at the first read
choices.why: Right: "report made" came first, then the line once.

choices.text: Once, when the instance is created
choices.why: It came after "report made", so creation did not build it.

choices.text: Zero times, as `print` is not allowed in a property
choices.why: The closure may do anything an ordinary one may.

prompt: Why is `let report = Report(…); print(report.summary)` refused when `summary` is `lazy` and `Report` is a struct?
hint: The compiler called it a mutating getter.

choices.text: A lazy property is private to the type that declares it, so outside code cannot read it
choices.why: Access control is lesson 17, and `lazy` changes nothing there.

choices.text: Lazy properties exist only on classes
choices.why: `Lazy.swift` used one on a struct held in a `var`.

choices.text: `summary` has no type annotation
choices.why: It has one, `String`.

choices.text: The first read stores a value, which is a change a `let` struct forbids
choices.why: Right: hold it in a `var`, or make the type a class.

prompt: Which of these is the best fit for `lazy`?
hint: Expensive, maybe never needed, and fixed once built.

choices.text: A formatter for a report screen many students never open
choices.why: Right: built on first use, kept after, and not built for those who never ask.

choices.text: A week's total that changes as sessions are added
choices.why: A lazy value is built once and would go stale; that is a computed property.

choices.text: The minutes of a session
choices.why: Cheap and always needed: a stored property.

choices.text: The weekly goal shared by all sessions
choices.why: Shared by the type: a `static let`.

prompt: The session type declares a constant with `static let`. How is it read?

choices.text: `monday.weeklyGoal`, through any instance
choices.why: Refused: `static member 'weeklyGoal' cannot be used on instance`.

choices.text: `StudySession.weeklyGoal`
choices.why: Right, or `Self.weeklyGoal` inside the type.

choices.text: `weeklyGoal`, from anywhere in the program
choices.why: Inside an instance method even that was refused.

choices.text: Only after an instance has been created
choices.why: `Static.swift` printed it before any session existed.

prompt: In `Static.swift`, `share()` divides a session's minutes by the weekly goal of 300. What does it return for 60 minutes?
Section 06 says a `static var` deserves care. Why?

choices.text: It is recomputed on every read
choices.why: It is stored, and initialised once.

choices.text: Each instance gets its own copy
choices.why: There is one for the whole type.

choices.text: It is a global variable shared by the whole program
choices.why: Right: any code may change it at any moment, which lesson 15's compiler refuses.

choices.text: Its first read is slow
choices.why: Speed is not the concern the section names.

prompt: A class has `let owner` and `var goal: Int`, and its `init` sets only `owner`. What happens?

choices.text: `goal` starts at 0
choices.why: Swift gives no implicit zero.

choices.text: `goal` is `nil` until set
choices.why: An `Int` is not optional, so it cannot be `nil`.

choices.text: Refused: not all stored properties initialised
choices.why: Right, with a note pointing at `self.goal`.

choices.text: A crash the first time anything reads `goal` while the program runs
choices.why: The compiler catches it first.

prompt: Where can you write a second `init` for a struct and keep the memberwise one?

choices.text: Inside the struct's braces, marked `convenience`
choices.why: `convenience` is a class word, and inside the braces the memberwise one goes.

choices.text: In an extension
choices.why: Right: `Extra.swift` used both.

choices.text: Nowhere; a struct has one or the other
choices.why: `Extra.swift` had both.

choices.text: In a separate file of the same program
choices.why: The file does not matter; the extension does.

prompt: What type is `StudySession(course: "Swift", typed: "45")` when that initialiser is `init?`?

choices.text: `StudySession`, as "45" is valid
choices.why: The type does not depend on the argument.

choices.text: `StudySession?`
choices.why: Right: every call may give `nil`, so the type says so.

choices.text: `Int?`
choices.why: That is what `Int(typed)` gives inside it.

choices.text: `Result<StudySession, Error>`
choices.why: `Result` is lesson 12, and `init?` gives an optional.

prompt: An initialiser that hands the work to another initialiser of the same type, as `self.init(course:minutes:)` did, is called ___.
Match each need of the planner to the kind of property that fits it.

pairs.left: A week's total, always in step with its sessions
Minutes that must never exceed 600 after a change
A costly summary built only if somebody reads it
The goal shared by every session

prompt: `session.minutes = 900` on a property with both observers and a clamp to 600. Put what happens in order.
A session must never exist with 0 minutes. Section 04's observer clamps changes. What does it miss, and what closes the gap?

choices.text: Reads; a computed property
choices.why: Reads cannot make a value invalid.

choices.text: Initialisation; an `init?` that refuses bad values
choices.why: Right: observers skip the initialiser, and a failable one checks before the value exists.

choices.text: Copies; a class instead of a struct
choices.why: A copy carries an already valid value.

choices.text: Nothing; the observer already covers every case a session can reach
choices.why: `StudySession(minutes: 0)` runs no observer.
